articles.title: Forensic expert says his analysis of autopsy photos suggests Epstein was killed
articles.summary: Professor Michael Freeman tells BBC Newsnight that he believes the convicted sex offender's injuries are consistent with a homicide.
body: Watch: Forensic expert Michael Freeman speaks to Newsnight about Epstein's death
This article contains distressing details and references to suicide
A forensic expert has said he believes that convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein's death in prison was the result of a homicide, not suicide.
Speaking to BBC Newsnight, Professor Michael Freeman said that after reviewing the New York City medical examiner's file he believes Epstein was strangled, most likely from behind.

The medical examiner who carried out the autopsy concluded in 2019 that Epstein's injuries were consistent with suicide and there was no evidence of the defensive wounds expected if his death had been a homicide.
Epstein was found dead in prison on 10 August 2019 in New York as he awaited trial on sex trafficking charges.

Dr Barbara Sampson, chief medical examiner at the time of Epstein's autopsy, who ruled that Epstein's death was a suicide, has previously said: "I stand firmly behind our determination of the cause and manner of death for Mr. Epstein." The BBC has approached Sampson for further comment.
Freeman has served as a cause-of-death expert to attorneys-general in the US for death in police custody cases, including George Floyd in Minnesota.
He published his research and the New York City medical examiner's files after presenting his findings in London on Monday evening.

Freeman, who did not see the body, based his conclusions on the files and photographs from the examiner's report provided to him by Epstein's brother, Mark Epstein, who has always maintained that his brother was murdered.
Freeman said his analysis is independent and that he was not paid by Mark Epstein. His research has not been peer reviewed.

He told the BBC that he believed there are signs indicating an assault on Epstein, including a deep haemorrhage to his left shoulder and injuries that appear to be consistent to being struck in the face.
Freeman said he believed the evidence was most consistent with strangulation using a ligature and then that same ligature was probably used to suspend the body from the bunk bed.

He said there appeared to be fingernail marks above the ligature mark on Epstein's neck, which "would be consistent with strangulation, particularly from behind. And the attempt by the victim to try to remove the ligature from the neck".
He said "the injuries and the way the body was found don't match up. There's only one remaining explanation then, and that is that the death was as a result of a homicide."

The medical examiner who performed the autopsy at the time told the Department of Justice (DoJ) Office of the Inspector General , externalthat Epstein's injuries were more consistent with, and indicative of, a suicide by hanging rather than homicide by strangulation, adding there was no evidence of defensive wounds consistent with what is seen in victims of strangulation.
Epstein was awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges when he was found dead in his cell
Freeman said he would have expected in an investigation of a death by hanging in custody for there to be a photograph before the body was taken down.

According to a DoJ investigation into Epstein's time in prison, the guard who found Epstein immediately called for a second colleague to help, lowered Epstein's body to the floor and began attempts to resuscitate him.
Epstein's death came a month after he was briefly placed on suicide watch, the DoJ report said.
When asked who might have killed Epstein if his interpretation of the evidence was correct, Freeman said he had "no idea".
"That is not something I have an opinion about. That isn't any part of any investigation that I've done," he said.
Challenged on whether his views veered into conspiracy theory, Freeman said: "I have the luxury of being able to say, don't take my word for it, let everybody look at it."

"If you think I'm still a conspiracy theorist because I'm looking at something that looks like a strangulation and say, I think it is a strangulation and I don't think it could be a hanging, show me where I got it wrong."
"I'm wide open to that. I'm an academic. I'm quite happy to hear people's theories on things that are informed," he said.
Epstein was convicted in 2008 of soliciting prostitution from a minor, for which he was registered as a sex offender. He escaped a heavy jail sentence as a result of a plea deal.

Eleven years later, Epstein was charged with running a network of underage girls for sex. He was awaiting trial in 2019 when he was found dead at the Metropolitan Correctional Center in New York City.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy to face retrial next year for deaths of her three children
articles.summary: The 36-year-old's first trial this year fell apart when a 12-person jury failed to reach a verdict.
body: Watch: Date announced for Lindsay Clancy retrial
Warning: This story contains details some readers may find distressing.
Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman accused of murdering her three children, will face a retrial next year, a judge has said, after a jury deadlocked last time in a case that gripped the nation.
The judge set a trial date for 29 March 2027, though the district attorney did not explicitly say what charges Clancy would face.
Prosecutors said they wanted a jury trial, and the defence said they took that to mean Clancy, 36, would again face first-degree murder charges.
Five-year-old Cora, Dawson, three, and eight-month-old Callan were strangled at the family home on 24 January 2023. The defence argues she had severe postpartum psychosis.

"I think you can read between the lines that when they say that the case is going to require a jury, that it's an indirect comment from the DA [district attorney] that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments, so we will pick a trial date," defence lawyer Kevin Reddington said at Monday's hearing.
Prosecutors wanted a May trial date, but Judge William Sullivan decided on March instead. The judge is due to retire in June.
Clancy was charged in the first trial with three counts of first-degree-murder, which is the intentional and premeditated killing of another person.
The district attorney has not yet officially said he will proceed with first-degree-murder charges. The BBC has contacted the district attorney's office for comment.
Clancy with her ex-husband and their children - five-year-old Cora, Dawson, three, and eight-month-old Callan

The prosecution could choose to bring lesser charges against Clancy, such as second-degree-murder, which applies to unlawful killings committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without planning.
A week ago, Judge Sullivan rejected a defence attempt to throw out the case on the grounds of double jeopardy.
Double jeopardy is a legal principle that protects someone from being prosecuted more than once for the same crime after an acquittal or conviction.
The judge's decision cleared the way for a second trial. It was Judge Sullivan who declared the mistrial on 4 September because of the hung jury.
Afterwards, some of the 12 jurors said in media interviews that they had been ready to find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity, but that one juror had held out.
It was not disputed at Clancy's first trial that she strangled the children with exercise bands in the basement of the family home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury.
She had asked her now-ex husband, Patrick Clancy, to leave the house to pick up takeout food and children's medicine shortly before the children were attacked.
The defence team wanted her found not guilty by reason of insanity, known in Massachusetts as lack of criminal responsibility.
The case sparked a debate over how postpartum mental illness is treated in the US.
Clancy is currently in a state-run psychiatric hospital and medical facility in Massachusetts.

articles.title: Five EU countries announce migrant deportation centre in Rwanda
articles.summary: Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands have announced a "return hub" for failed asylum seekers.
body: Five EU countries will open a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda next year as part of a broader push to boost removals.
Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to open a "return hub" ready to accept transfers in 2027, the Dutch and Danish governments announced in statements.

The countries said the scheme would apply to migrants staying illegally in their nations who are subject to deportation, with the Dutch government adding it will provide an alternative if deportees cannot be returned to their country of origin.
Deportees will be able to either integrate into Rwandan society or return to their home country, the nations said.

The scheme will apply to people who have exhausted their legal avenues to stay in the five nations - unlike a scrapped British deal that envisaged sending people to Rwanda to have their claims processed. Legal challenges meant the UK deal never took off, and it was eventually junked by the incoming Labour government in 2024.
Downing Street has not ruled out the UK joining the scheme, saying they will watch it "with interest".
The five countries say the plan to send migrants abroad is in line with EU and international law, but human rights bodies say it could violate migrant rights.
The deal follows a recent EU reform that allowed for the creation of hubs outside of the bloc.

In a joint press conference in Vienna on Monday, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said the five countries wanted to relieve European asylum systems and stop traffickers arranging deadly trips across the Mediterranean.

In a written statement, the Dutch government said the five countries will "only return single men" as part of the first phase of the deal, adding that the focus for the Netherlands "will be on persons from countries of origin in the same region as Rwanda".
Once in Rwanda, people will be able to integrate into society, which means they will have the right of residence, as well as access to education, healthcare, the labour market and the legal system.
Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said the country is commmited to working with European partners to provide a "safe, legal and dignified solution for migrants".
He added that they would also work on "correcting the global imbalance in economic opportunities", which he called a "key driver of irregular migration".

Ahead of the announcement, diplomatic sources told the AFP news agency the hub is expected to initially run as a pilot, hosting about 100 people, with each of the five nations possibly sending about 20 migrants.
The United Nations' International Organisation for Migration (IOM) could play an ancillary role.

"IOM has a long history of providing assistance to migrants in situations of transit, including in complex contexts," an IOM spokesperson said, adding the agency was in discussions with some EU countries "on plans for the establishment of return hubs or similar mechanisms".
With elections approaching in several EU nations, administrations have been under pressure to show they can control migration.
Concerns around security, struggling economies and disillusionment with governing parties have all had a major role in shaping attitudes towards people leaving their home countries.

Human Rights Watch's senior Africa researcher Clementine de Montjoye said the choice of Rwanda would be a cause of concern as it had a "well-established record of repression of dissent, arbitrary detention, ill-treatment in detention" and support for armed rebels in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo.

"Paying Kigali to host a deportation programme would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad."

The independent EU Agency for Fundamental Rights argued any third country hosting a return hub should "respect fundamental rights", including that people should not be sent to a country where they face serious risk of persecution.
Unaccompanied children should not be sent to a return hub, the agency said.

According to the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, there were almost 110,000 irregular border crossings into the EU in the first 10 months of 2026, which represents a 29% decrease compared to the previous year.

In October, about 18,100 crossings were detected, which is about 6% less than October 2025 but 22% more than in September "largely because of a sharp rise in arrivals on the Western African route to the Canary Islands".

articles.title: New Zealand tricks and annual leave - the lengths fans are going to for GTA 6
articles.summary: Sensor Tower estimates the game has already made $1.18bn from pre-orders across PlayStation and Xbox
body: GTA 6 will feature a playable female character for the first time since the 2D games

After 13 years of waiting, some GTA 6 fans are taking extra steps to play the game - from booking time off work, buying a console to play it on or even pretending they're halfway around the world to get early access.
Market intelligence firm Sensor Tower estimates, external GTA 6 has already generated $1.18bn (£894m) from 12 million pre-orders - although Rockstar has not confirmed this.

Despite the option to preload the 212GB game, Jennifer Holmes, chief executive of the London Internet Exchange, said several UK internet providers including BT and Virgin Media had "increased capacity in anticipation of higher demand" ahead of launch.
But for some fans, simply having the game ready to play is not enough.
GTA 6 - all you need to know about Rockstar's blockbuster game
Gamers have long been known to book time off work for major releases.

When Red Dead Redemption 2 launched in October 2018, social media users were sharing plans to take the day off, with one analytics firm reportedly finding, external more people talking about calling in sick for it than any other game that year.
Similar conversations took place ahead of Cyberpunk 2077's release in December 2020, with fans discussing , externaltaking several days off to play.
GTA 6 is no exception, but it appears to characteristically be taking things to a whole new level.
For the game's launch day, HR software company BrightHR, external looked at absence data from more than 1.2 million employees from 70,000 businesses across the UK.
It found GTA was mentioned in 4.6% of time-off requests by employees. Throughout November and December, it said an estimated 83,000 days had been booked off for the game.

According to the HR firm, one person put "new GTA is coming out! I will be spending a week on the sofa in my pants!" as the reason for their leave request, while another said: "play the new GTA - I've waited a billion years".
A third said in their request: "GTA Release - I'll put my notice in if this is denied."
The company added it had no way of tracking if the requests had actually been approved by employers.
GTA 6 is set in a fictional state inspired by Florida, which has featured heavily in the game's marketing, including this promotional blimp.
Some places have even decided to lean into the trend by offering incentives around the game – including the US Army's 3rd Infantry Division based at Fort Stewart, Georgia.

It gave some active-duty soldiers a four-day pass to play the game when it is released in November, as long as they sign a reenlistment contract for a minimum of two years between 1 August and 12 November.

"The idea was to have a unique incentives programme that connects to what soldiers are interested in," public affairs officer for the division, Lieutenant Colonel Angel Tomko confirmed to the BBC in August.
"There are 130 soldiers eligible within the battalion, and 20 have selected this incentive as part of their reenlistment," she said at the time.

You may want to read Meta’s Instagram cookie policy, external and privacy policy, external before accepting. To view this content choose ‘accept and continue’.
Aside from taking time off, some gamers have also been discussing a technical loophole which could give them valuable extra hours of play before it officially unlocks in their country.

Because GTA 6 will release at midnight local time in all regions, New Zealand will become one of the first places where it is available, due to it reaching midnight earliest because of its position near the international date line.
This has led to some investigating ways to "trick" their consoles into thinking they're based in the island country when they are in fact thousands of miles away.
According to Google Trends, searches for the "GTA 6 New Zealand trick" have surged by more than 5,000% in the UK over the past month.
Games journalist Vic Hood said many gamers would be looking to play earlier to "get in on the action as soon as possible", as well as to prevent spoilers.
"As New Zealand is 13 hours ahead of the UK, that's 13 hours of gameplay that has time to spread across the internet and potentially spoil some key story beats and in-game surprises," she said.
"Took an extra day of paid time off when I found this out," one fan posted on Reddit on the trick.
It also means gamers would be playing the game at the much nicer time of 11:00 GMT, rather than having to stay up all night.

But another Xbox user shared caution on Reddit, noting that while the loophole had been exploited for many years for other game releases, GTA 6 "might be the game where Microsoft finally does something about this 'exploit'" - which could include banning players.
GTA 6's developers Rockstar and publishers Take Two Interactive have not commented on the loophole, and neither has Sony nor Microsoft.

Louise Wooldridge from analyst firm Ampere Analysis said both Microsoft and Sony had "rules governing regional accounts and purchases" for the Xbox and PlayStation, adding that Sony's were "slightly more restrictive".
Players who choose to use the workaround could therefore risk breaching those terms and conditions and potentially face restrictions on their accounts or lose access to their digital games.
The hype for the game has taken over locations across the world, including Selfridges in London
Some gamers will have to wait even longer than their console-playing counterparts to get their hands on GTA 6, as the game will not be available on PC at launch, similar to previous GTA releases.
"Spare a thought for the PC users who will have to live vicariously through others' YouTube videos and Twitch streams," gamer Stephen Finn told the BBC.
A PS5 now costs from £520, while the more powerful PS5 Pro is nearly £790.
Despite the hefty price tag, for some the temptation to join the community in playing what many have called the biggest game launch of the year, if not decade, has been too great.
Reddit posts and videos, such as one by US YouTuber isoish, external, show fans buying consoles specifically to play the game.
"So, the only game I'm going to have on here is GTA," the content creator said in the video.
After more than a decade of waiting, it seems some fans are determined not to waste a single minute of GTA 6's release - no matter what the cost or extra effort.

articles.title: Trump says Alaska voters chose the wrong Dan Sullivan. What does the data show?
articles.summary: Votes are still being counted in the Alaska Senate race, with Democrat Mary Peltola ahead of Republican incumbent Senator Dan S Sullivan.
body: Almost two weeks after the Democrats swept to victory in the midterm elections, votes are still being counted in the race to elect a senator in Alaska, with Democratic candidate Mary Peltola ahead of her Republican rival - Senator Dan S Sullivan.
This Senate contest has drawn scrutiny after another Dan Sullivan entered the race earlier this year - with ballot papers listing both the incumbent Dan S Sullivan and a Daniel J Sullivan Jr.

Republicans have said this could have confused voters, prompting an unsuccessful legal challenge and President Donald Trump claiming votes for "the fake Dan Sullivan" were supposed to be for "the real Dan Sullivan".
US media has not forecasted a winner in the race - the last Senate seat still without a winner after the 3 November election.
But with 98% of the vote counted, even if Senator Dan S Sullivan's votes were combined with Daniel J Sullivan Jr's votes, this would still not overcome Peltola's lead.

Alaska uses a ranked-choice voting system, which means voters can vote for five candidates in order of preference. If no candidate reaches more than 50% of the first preference votes, then voters' other choices will be used to decide who wins.
BBC Verify has analysed voting data showing voters' second choices. It shows that over a third of voters who put Daniel J Sullivan Jr first left their second choice blank.
The next highest second-choice preference was for the Democratic candidate Mary Peltola - receiving nearly twice as many second-choice votes as the Republican Dan S Sullivan.
This calls into question claims that Republican voters may have been confused about which Sullivan they were voting for.
Why midterm vote-counting is taking so long in America's largest state
Republican Dan S Sullivan has held the US Senate seat in Alaska since 2015 and was running for his third term.
Daniel J Sullivan Jr - a retired school teacher from a remote fishing village in Alaska - entered the race in May and has run a low-key campaign.

A New York Times story, external published the week before Election Day claimed that Democratic operatives with links to the Peltola campaign had tried to recruit "spoiler" candidates in the Senate race, including Daniel J Sullivan Jr.

The report said it had seen text messages and interviewed 12 people who participated in or were told of the plan, or were would-be candidates who the team also tried to recruit. The BBC has not independently verified the reporting.
Peltola has denied all knowledge of the alleged "scheme" and Sullivan Jr has denied any links with the Peltola campaign.
President Trump has posted multiple times on Truth Social since the election, claiming that the race has been "rigged".
But experts note it's not an illegal tactic, if it was employed.
"There is nothing to prevent a campaign from recruiting someone else to run, even if for political reasons," said Joshua Douglas, an election law expert at the University of Kentucky.
Alaska Senate candidate denies knowing about alleged plot to put two Dan Sullivans on ballot
Senator Sullivan was joined by President Trump at a campaign rally ahead of the vote
Voters in Alaska select their first choice candidate, followed by options to rank up to four other candidates in order of preference.

"There is no specific law preventing people with the same name running, but many states have laws or regulations about how names appear on the ballot. One of those regulations was used in Alaska" said Ruth Greenwood, director of the election law clinic at Harvard Law School.
On Alaskans' ballots the two Sullivans were listed as:
- Sullivan, Dan S. (Registered Republican) Incumbent
There was a second registered Republican candidate, Gerald Heikes - who was also allegedly recruited into the race according to The New York Times.
A sample ballot for the US Senate election in Alaska
As of Tuesday, Peltola holds 49.98% of the vote.

In the event that Peltola were not to clear 50%, officials eliminate the candidate in last place and reallocate those ballots to the voters' next choices. This process continues until two candidates remain, with one clearing the 50% hurdle.
Daniel J Sullivan Jr is the listed candidate in last place with 1.65% of the vote.
Democrat Mary Peltola's said on Saturday she will "decisively be elected" as Alaska's next senator
Senator Dan S Sullivan and his allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters.
Trump said last week: "Anybody that voted for that second Dan Sullivan, the fake Dan Sullivan, was supposed to be a vote for the real Dan Sullivan".
Of the ballots analysed by BBC Verify that ranked Daniel J Sullivan Jr first, 38% of them recorded no valid second choice.
We do not know how many of these voters may have thought they had voted for the Senator Dan S Sullivan and then not ranked any other candidates.
A further 29% of Daniel J Sullivan Jr voters ranked the Democratic candidate Mary Peltola second, almost double the 15% that ranked the incumbent Republican Senator Sullivan as second.

"The likelihood that any confusion might play a significant role is diminished in Alaska," Richard Pildes, a professor of constitutional law at New York University, argues, "because any voter who was unsure which Dan Sullivan candidate they meant to vote for could rank them first and second."

articles.title: China is hosting the world's leaders in its AI wonderland. Here's what they won't see
articles.summary: Leave Shenzhen's tech-flecked city skyline and you run into the challenges confronting Xi's China.
body: Watch: The two sides of daily life in Shenzhen
At 27, Huang Shihua is living the Chinese Dream.

He works as an engineer for a leading humanoid robot company in Shenzhen. The sprawling south-eastern metropolis is touted by China as the origin story for a high-tech future powered by artificial intelligence, robotics and home-grown innovation.

Drones soar across the sky to deliver your dinner, driverless taxis play relaxing music as you journey to your destination, and robots don't just hand you a cappuccino - they explain the origin of your coffee beans.

"We have created a miracle in Shenzhen," Huang says, surrounded by humanoid robots making coffee and playing chess. "Many young people from across China, full of passion and dreams, have flocked here."
Now they all spend their days figuring out ways to make robots smarter.
Shenzhen, China's AI-powered "city of dreams", has long been a place of opportunity
The Chinese call Shenzhen the "city of dreams". The moniker suits it: one of China's wealthiest, it is close to Hong Kong and the place where the country's explosive growth took off decades ago.

Its manufacturing inventory mirrors China's rise: cabbage patch dolls, then TVs, later iPhones, electric vehicles, drones and now the robots, which are drawing Huang and a new generation of Chinese ambition.

The "miracles" these young engineers are chasing are central to Xi Jinping's bold vision for China. So where better to show it off than Shenzhen, which will be centre-stage when US President Donald Trump, Russian leader Vladimir Putin and others arrive for a global economic summit this week.

And yet there is another side to this flashy, coastal city, a side that they will not get to see. Drive away from towering skyscrapers towards Shajing and Songgang, once the source of much of the world's electronics, and you will run into the challenges confronting Xi's China.
Young, ambitious developers have turned Shenzhen into a "miracle", Huang says
"Everyone feels life is hard," one construction worker tells us. "Lots of factories have relocated and workers lost their jobs."

China remains exceptionally good at making things - and Shenzhen is proof of that. But the city also holds the evidence for what ails the world's second-largest economy. The property crisis is not over, denting confidence in the future. This is one of China's most expensive cities but even here, our taxi driver tells us, his house is now only worth a third of its original price.

A weak property market and sluggish consumer spending mean many households are buying less. Factories are increasingly relying on exports while many manufacturers have cut production, downsized, automated or moved elsewhere in search of cheaper labour.
The result is a growing number of workers turning to temporary jobs in the gig economy, often with lower pay and fewer benefits.
"Shenzhen is not a magic place," says one delivery driver in his 40s, unwilling to give his name.
"Some say there is gold everywhere in Shenzhen, but it's not like that anymore. It's not a city where you can come and thrive. If you don't work hard, you won't have anything."

The BBC spent several days in Shenzhen exploring these two very different sides of China's progress: on the one hand is the dazzling promise of AI, and on the other are the anxieties of workers who worry if there will be room for them in the future it creates.
Delivery drones in Shenzhen have become a tourist attraction
Wednesday is sandwich and bubble tea day in the offices of DexForce Technologies.

The elevator is packed with young engineers and developers headed to the right floor for the free carbs and sugar that will fuel their afternoon. They jostle past their creations en route: human-sized, yellow robots whose limbs fill every available corner.

"I believe that in a decade, robots will be able to better serve humanity by taking on highly repetitive or even dangerous tasks," Huang says. That could be anything from serving coffee to working in mines, and they are being trained for all of that in this laboratory for the future, where machines flail, jerk or lurch into motion as they learn to behave.
To him, "Shenzhen is another 'America'. Because, much like in the US, many young people have been able to realise their dreams and earn the wealth they desire."

This is what Xi wants to hear as he pushes China to lead the world in advanced tech. Shenzhen has indeed long been a place for seeking opportunity but Huang and his colleagues want to do much more. They don't simply want to continue China's manfuacturing supremacy. They want to transform it.
DexForce Technologies is brimming with robots - and faith in a tech-charged future

Beyond making "our lives more convenient and comfortable", Huang sees AI as helping "the entire world become one family - a global village. AI has the potential to foster equality and the prospect of AI-driven equality is, to me, the most exciting possibility of all."
Smiling enthusiastically, he explains how he hopes that robots can help emerging economies across Africa and South East Asia catch up by reshaping their production lines too.

This tech-charged optimism, which is everywhere in the building, jars with the uncertainty elsewhere in Shenzhen, where robots are nowhere to be found. Yet. But that's just the first of the differences.
In Huang's side of the city, tech and finance workers stroll to the office after a morning workout, sipping coffee that probably cost more than 30 yuan ($4.50; £3.40).
On the other side, scooters whizz through streets piled high with goods being shuttled between factories as vendors sell whole breakfast plates of spicy noodles for under 3 yuan.
The two sides of Shenzhen are a contrast in more ways than one
Outside one of the city's tallest skyscrapers, 50-year-old Ms Lu has a phone to her ear and a pen in her right hand while grabbing a bag with her left from a delivery driver.
She shouts four key numbers at her co-worker: instructions for another Chinese woman who is waiting to take the delivery up the elevator to someone sitting at their desk.

This is the lunchtime rush outside SEG plaza, home to 70 storeys of thousands of tenants. Lu used to be one of them. "I ran a small business on the second floor. I sold circuit boards," she says. "But it's getting so hard to do business these days and the rental fees got higher."

Often likened to China's Silicon Valley, Shenzhen has seen rents soar with the influx of new capital, squeezing out smaller, more traditional businesses. At 50, Ms Lu couldn't find another job until the delivery drivers came to her with a plan.
The wait for the elevator can take half an hour – wasted money for a driver trying to fill as many orders as possible. So Ms Lu became a new layer in the ever-evolving gig economy.

"The delivery drivers bring food here to the building entrance. We pick it up and take it upstairs. The drivers pay us 2 yuan per order," she explains, always on the move. Delivery drivers earn between four to eight yuan per order, so Ms Lu gets a decent cut of their earnings.

"The lunch peak time only lasts two or three hours… if they use our service, they can get more orders done, and we can earn some money as well. But the market is bad. These days I only earn around 200 yuan per day."
Ms Lu, standing in the middle, joined the delivery business after losing her job

An estimated 200 million Chinese workers, roughly 40% of the urban labour force, now depend on some form of gig work. Many delivery drivers in Shenzhen tell us they chose temporary work because there are fewer opportunities at factories than before.

"We need to adapt to the situation we find ourselves in," one driver told us, "rather than waiting for it to adapt to our needs." A group of them are waiting outside the gates of an e-cigarette factory to make industrial deliveries.
Others nod in agreement. Another driver says he has little choice: "I have two children to raise and I can't stop working. I don't have time to think about anything else."
Permanent jobs often require contributions to social security and pension, which reduces take-home pay. But gig work means more cash in hand and flexibile hours.

"Most workers prefer jobs with a fixed, shorter-term duration. It allows them the flexibility to resign and leave whenever they choose; they have no desire to become permanent employees," says job agent Li Xiaohe.
Increasingly, he puts up boards on pavements advertising temporary factory jobs that pay around 22 yuan an hour for assembling small electronics.
Although agents also appear to be in a shrinking pool, with several former shop fronts shuttered: yet another sign of the downturn in traditional manufacturing.
"Our business is perhaps not as optimistic as it once was," Li admits. "We can feel the effects of Shenzhen going through a transformation."
Li, a labour agent who advertises temporary jobs, says his own business has been struggling
That transformation is hard to miss.

Drones buzz above the lush grounds of a purpose built "talent park" along the city's waterfront, dipping and darting as they deliver meals to a dedicated platform. Phones held high, tourists capture them landing with their lunch.

"This is amazing. The technology is just great. I wish we had this back at home," exclaims one Canadian tourist. Our coffee order - for a five-yuan delivery - arrives in just over 15 minutes, the drone landing seamlessly so I can pick up my order.

"I heard that many years ago, Shenzhen was a fishing village," says Anle, who is visiting from Vietnam. "Ha – no more fishing village," he laughs as he orders milk tea to be delivered by drone for him and his wife.

For all the ingenuity on display, it feels more like a demonstration of what is possible rather than a mundane reality. The deliveries, which are only possible in certain locations, stop at 20:00 local time. The driverless cars, which need a separate app to order, are also a novelty – they even offer you a massage when you are on your way.
At night, in the glow of a thousand dancing lights, the drones take on a different role. They fly above the park warning people to behave and not cause trouble.
Shenzhen still draws millions of migrant workers from across China
Far from the glittering skyline, workers gather around plastic tables outside restaurants serving cheap hotpot and seafood skewers.
There are more expensive restaurants along the street, but they too have taken a hit. One owner told us business is down by more than 70% as workers are hesitant to splurge on dinner.
Many of them have spent decades here, including 58-year-old construction worker Mr Wu. He arrived in Shenzhen from Sichuan in the 1990s not long after China opened the city up to foreign businesses.
He was among millions of migrants from poorer provinces who came to work on production lines or build skyscrapers. They are still coming.

articles.title: Taking Korea's toughest exam from behind bars
articles.summary: Eleven convicts at the Mandela Boys' School will be among the thousands of young Koreans taking the country's hardest exam, the Suneung.
body: The boys in Mandela have been convicted of serious offences
Students intently focus on maths formulas written on a board before lowering their heads and taking notes as the teacher works through a sum.
The teacher's voice and the scratch of pens fill the room.
At first glance, this could be any classroom in South Korea.
But thick metal bars cover the windows and the students are wearing blue prison uniforms and rubber shoes emblazoned with the words "Korea Correctional Service".

This is Mandela Boys' School, an education facility for young prisoners inside the Seoul Southern Correctional Institution in Guro, south-west Seoul. In South Korea, young people who are sentenced to imprisonment by a criminal court must serve their time in prison.

"The boys here have committed serious offences and received criminal sentences," Jeong Yeo-gyeong, a correctional officer in the Korea Correctional Service's social reintegration division, told the BBC.
"As well as theft, there is a high proportion of serious offences, including violence, bodily injury, sexual violence and robbery."
But by opening educational institutes like Mandela, authorities are hoping to give these young offenders a chance to better their lives after they serve out their sentences.

Opened by the justice ministry in March 2023, it allows boys who were aged 17 and under when their sentences became final to prepare for school equivalency exams as well as the Suneung - the country's notoriously difficult university entrance examination - while still serving their sentences.
Held every November, the Suneung is an infamous eight-hour marathon of back-to-back exams.
Students attempt about 200 questions across various subjects, which include Korean, maths, English, social and natural sciences, among others.
The country itself comes to a standstill - construction work halts, planes are grounded and military training gets suspended to facilitate an optimal testing environment.
A total of 551,864 people have applied to take this year's Suneung on 19 November.
Around 30 prisoners are enrolled in the Suneung preparation class at Mandela Boys' School, and 11 of them have applied to take this year's exam.
Several boys are sitting the Suneung exam this year and are taking intensive preparation classes
Park Soo-young (not his real name), a 17-year-old inmate, has been at the Mandela Boys' Suneung preparation class for two months and hopes to study social welfare.
He tells the BBC that he had dreams of becoming a police officer before committing the crime that landed him behind bars.
He says he could not bring himself to look properly at his mother during his trial. When he turned towards her after his sentence was announced, she was crying.

"Seeing her like that, I broke down too. I wondered how I was going to live from then on, and how I could look after my mother, who was on her own. I think I kept crying for about a week while I was in the detention centre."

Looking back on his offence, he says he feels "very ashamed that I couldn't control that impulse". If he could meet his younger self, he would tell him: "Control that impulse. If you do, everything will be different."
"I'd grab myself by the collar and shake myself as I said it."
He hopes the Suneung and university will offer him a chance to start again.

"Once I'm out, I need to cut ties with the friends and people I used to know and start a new life. I think university is the only way to do that. Going to university would let me leave the area where I used to live, move somewhere else and start something new. That's why I began studying again."
But he describes beginning Suneung preparation as "a struggle every day".
"But the teachers don't let anything slip past. They keep helping us until we understand. If I don't understand something, I put my hand up and they come over and explain it.
Sometimes, if I've missed something, I keep working at it on my own. If I still can't get it, I ask the students next to me to explain," he said.
Park's day begins at 06:30 with a morning check by prison officers. He starts memorising English vocabulary and working through Korean reading passages early in the morning.

"I learn English words whenever I can, even before breakfast. From 07:00, I work through a Korean passage, something like literature or speech. We have to come down to the classroom at 08:00, so we have another check and then come down for lessons."

During breaks, students make calls to their families or leave the classroom for scheduled visits. In the evening, they return for supervised study. Once the day's activities are over, they must go back to their cells together.
Park says he studies until 22:00 before finishing for the day. If he wants to study longer hours, he needs permission from a prison officer.

But even if gets a good result this year, Park will not be allowed to leave prison and attend university straight away. He is only due to be released in 2028, but plans to use this exam as experience and continue studying next year.
"This time, I want to experience how the Suneung works and how competitive it is. Then, next year, I'll work hard from the start so I can get in the year after that."
By opening educational institutes like Mandela, authorities are hoping to give young offenders a chance to better their lives
Some former students from Mandela Boys' School have managed to get into university, according to the justice ministry.
Others have continued their studies after leaving prison, including by enrolling in residential exam preparation academies.
The inmates are taught by a team of seven prison officers, all of whom hold teaching certificates. Each is responsible for a subject.
Visiting instructors provide classes in the humanities, arts and sport, while university student volunteers help with learning. Professional psychological counselling is also available.
Park Min-yong, who applied to work here in 2023, teaches science. And alongside Suneung lessons, he works with the students' to change their habits and behaviour.
One thing he often tells them is that they need to "learn how to become adults".

He believes that while studying in itself does not necessarily turn inmates away from a life of crime, the experience of having worked hard at something: staying with a concept that makes little sense, revisiting a wrong answer and continuing even when grades do not improve straight away, is valuable in itself.
"Studying properly means pushing yourself to your limits, and that takes considerable stamina and patience," he says.
"Whether they chose to do it or not, the experience of persevering, enduring and not giving up easily may help them to some extent when they face the difficulties of life after release."
He says the material they encounter while preparing for the Suneung also gives them new things to think about.

Korean reading passages cover literature, society, science and philosophy. Students have to consider a character's perspective, examine the evidence behind an argument and understand unfamiliar concepts. They also encounter explanations that differ from their own and have to reconsider what they think.
"They gradually learn that it's not just about their own personal view - that these concepts and relationships have been developed through a shared understanding among many people," Park said.
There are difficult moments too.
Park says students sometimes cheat in classroom tests even while he is watching.

"They cheat as if it's nothing. They give each other answers, even when I'm watching them. Some repeat it after being told off. There may be an element of doing it deliberately, but often they haven't thought it through. They don't think about the impact their actions or words could have on others."
The boys also have a strong desire for recognition, he says.
"It's all the time. 'Look how much I've done. Look how much my grades have improved. I've done this much - haven't I done well?' They're always like that. They're hungry for it."
Park Min-yong teaches science to the boys in Mandela
Not everyone agrees with this initiative though.

One criticism is that young people who have not committed crimes also face fierce competition for university places: so there is some anger that the state provides offenders with separate education and opportunities to prepare for this exam.
Father Jeong Min-ha, of the Archdiocese of Seoul's correctional ministry committee, worked with Seoul Southern Correctional Institution from September 2023 until last year.
He acknowledges these criticisms.
"Studying gives them a sense of achievement and time to look seriously at their own lives. That's why I think it matters. I think that is the most important part of rehabilitation."
Of course, there is no guarantee.
Park recalls a student who had done well at the school but later returned to prison.
"He was doing well when he left, but in the end he came back. So something went wrong. I'd hoped he would carry on with what he'd been doing here, but he couldn't. That's disappointing."

articles.title: BBC launches programme for children forced from school by bandits and poverty in West Africa
articles.summary: The new show brings English, maths and science lessons to children via TV, radio and social media.
body: Hadiza left school at 13 to get married and now spends her time doing housework
As she pounds millet, 15-year-old Hadiza sings the English alphabet. It is a reminder of something that she desperately misses - going to school.
"Sometimes I write on the ground to practise and see if I'm still writing correctly," she says.
One night, about two years ago, a group of armed men raided her village.
"They scared our cattle away and abducted a girl. We had to run away. We walked barefoot all the way here," she says.

Since then she has lived in a displaced persons camp in Goronyo, a few kilometres from her home. For a short while she went to school here, but soon met a young man and, at the age of 13, stopped going to classes and got married.
"It's tradition here that once a girl is married, her education ends," she explains.
Now she lives with her in-laws and helps look after the home.
Although Nigerian law prohibits marriage under the age of 18, it is not always enforced.
Hadiza practises writing on the ground to make sure she doesn't forget the English alphabet

Hadiza is one of nearly 19 million children in Nigeria who are missing out on an education, according to estimates shared by Unesco in 2024. That's about one in four of the country's school-age children.

Against this backdrop, the BBC World Service has launched Dars Hausa, an educational programme in the main language spoken in northern Nigeria, as well as neighbouring Niger, Cameroon and elsewhere in West Africa.

It brings English, maths and science lessons to children across West Africa, via social media, local television partnerships and radio. Many people in the region get their news from the radio and nearly half of households in Nigeria have one, according to the charity Save the Children.
Dars means "lesson" in Pashto and Dari, and it was first launched in those languages in 2023 for Afghan children barred from attending school. An Arabic version followed in February 2025.
The reasons why so many Nigerian children are out of school are numerous and complex. Like Hadiza, 12-year-old Rukayya also lives in the displacement camp in Goronyo.
After Rukayya's father was killed, she gave up school to earn money instead
"It pains me to see other children studying and going to school while I cannot," she says.
As the eldest child, each day Rukayya goes out to gather firewood to sell and to beg so that her younger siblings can have something to eat.
"If my father was alive, I wouldn't have to go out and beg," she explains, saying some people mock her "but it doesn't stop me because it is our only way to survive."
Bandits killed her father about a year ago in front of her, she says, and her family fled from their home to the camp.

She and Hadiza are among 670,000 people in north-west and central Nigeria who have been forced from their homes by armed robbery and kidnappings, according to the International Organization for Migration.
Three Girls: Lessons in Limbo features the stories of Hadiza and Rukayya - you can watch the full film on YouTube, external
Some attacks have been carried out by militant Islamist groups, but the majority in this region are by criminal gangs, known in Nigeria as bandits, who steal, kill and kidnap.
The school that Hadiza once attended in Goronyo is the only one serving children in the camp and typically has about 50 students in each class.

One of the teachers, Kamilu Sulaiman Jakada, says that even though lessons are free, only a tiny portion of the children attend, and even then sporadically, because parents tell him that "it is the children that are the breadwinners" and they need to earn money to eat.
Armed gangs, poverty and lack of funding all have a huge impact on children's education, says teacher Kamilu Sulaiman Jakada
He says the school does not have enough teachers or classrooms, explaining that funding is inconsistent and often comes from individuals or organisations rather than the government.

The other challenge is the bandits. A gang once came to the school on motorbikes, shooting in the air, he says, and although no-one was hurt, many parents were scared and withdrew their children. That has been parents' reaction to attacks in some other parts of the country too.
Every Nigerian child is meant to get nine years of free, compulsory education - six in primary and three in secondary school. Responsibility is shared between federal, state and local governments.
But many schools are facing shortages and poorer families who cannot afford private education can struggle to pay for uniforms, books and transport.
The crisis has built up over decades, with successive governments struggling to address chronic underfunding and poor oversight of resources.
In addition, many children in the traditional Almajiri system, which provides Islamic education, are not taught subjects such as maths and science, and are considered by Unicef to be out of school.
Many of Nigeria's schools face shortages of teachers, classrooms and learning materials after years of underfunding and lack of oversight

Minister of State for Education Prof Suwaiba Sa'id believes the number of children out of school is lower than has been reported, but admits that with Nigeria's growing population "the proper investment, the proper oversight, has not been done… I will not mention the names, but we know of two states that did not recruit a single teacher for eight years".

She says that education is the government's "number-one priority" and initiatives such as Lumina are designed to help address "decades of neglect". Lumina aims to support one million girls by 2030, providing an accelerated learning programme for older girls who have missed years of formal education.
She also says that "the government is doing everything possible" to deal with bandits and that "we have seen children that should be at school but are engaged in this banditry".

In the meantime, it is children like Hadiza and Rukayya that the BBC World Service Dars Hausa programmes aim to help. Hadiza says she still has a dream to one day become a doctor "to help my fellow women".

Dars Hausa will air on BBC News Hausa radio on Sundays at 06:45 West Africa Time, with a repeat at 20:45. The programme will also be available via BBC News Hausa's digital platforms, including YouTube, Facebook, X and Instagram.

articles.title: Ukraine critically damages Kerch Bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia
articles.summary: Photos of bridge, built after 2014 annexation and viewed by Ukraine as illegal, suggest massive steel arch has fallen into water
body: Ukraine has critically damaged the Kerch Bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia in an overnight missile attack, in what Volodymyr Zelenskyy hailed as an “unprecedented” military operation.

Footage showed a Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missile seconds before it hit the road and railway crossing, followed by an explosion. The strike follows an earlier attack on Monday that targeted an arch across its central section.

Writing on social media, the Ukrainian president described the attack as “a response to Russian strikes on our infrastructure”. He said it was the culmination of a long and complex campaign to demolish the bridge, involving domestically produced drones and ballistic missiles.

“Our warriors gradually destroyed air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective,” he wrote. “Palianytsia” drones hit the road section of the bridge, while Neptune and other missiles targeted the adjacent rail section, he added.

Earlier, Russian forces struck ⁠two major bridges in Kyiv that straddle the Dnipro River late on Monday, along with some other critical infrastructure, amid drone ⁠and missile attacks ​across Ukraine.

Ukraine has declared that the Kerch Bridge, built eight years ago after Vladimir Putin’s 2014 annexation of Crimea and known officially as the Crimean Bridge, is illegal. It has repeatedly attempted to destroy it, using a truck bomb in 2022 and a sea drone strike the following year.
The latest drone and missile barrage appears to have succeeded after months in which Ukrainian unmanned systems forces have systematically knocked out the peninsula’s multi-layered air defences.

The Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov, confirmed that the bridge, which was temporarily closed on Monday, was no longer usable. “The enemy has once again attacked the Crimean Bridge. At the moment, traffic has been suspended,” he posted on Telegram.
He added: “We ask residents and visitors in Crimea to refrain from travelling toward the bridge and to take these restrictions into account when planning their routes.”

Photos on Tuesday suggest that a 227-metre road arch span has fallen into the Kerch strait, which connects the Sea of Azov with the Black Sea. The adjacent railway arch span has also sustained damage.

Ukrainian commentators say the massive steel arch cannot easily be replaced. The closure of the bridge means traffic from Crimea can travel out of the peninsula only via a land corridor through occupied southern Ukraine, vulnerable to Ukrainian drones.

The debris appears to have blocked the main navigable route beneath the bridge, used by maritime traffic from the Sea of Azov and the ports of Berdiansk and Mariupol. The channel is 120 metres wide and 8.3 metres deep. Submerged steel struts could prevent large vessels from passing until the debris is removed.

The Russian government convened an emergency meeting to assess the attack, after which one of the country’s deputy prime ministers, Marat Khusnullin, briefed Putin on the damage to the bridge, according to the Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov.
Peskov added that the bridge would be repaired and would be “even better than before”, in comments to the Russian newspaper Izvestia.

But pro-war Russian commentators acknowledged that repairing the bridge would be very difficult, warning that, unlike in 2022 and 2023, Ukraine now had the capability to strike floating cranes and repair crews.
“Even installing a prefabricated arch under such conditions would be a formidable challenge,” wrote the influential Rybar Telegram channel, with close links to the defence ministry.

Ukrainian observers were gleeful at the bridge’s long-awaited destruction. They also pointed out that Ukraine’s armed forces could hit the bridge again to prevent repair work from being carried out. Serhii Sternenko, a former adviser to the defence ministry in Kyiv, wrote: “In response to your many questions. Yes, the bridge is fucked.”

Ukrainian blogger Anton Gerashchenko pointed out that Putin personally opened the bridge in 2018, driving across it in a Kamaz truck. “The Kerch bridge stands as the primary symbol of the Russian occupation of Ukrainian Crimea and the embodiment of its illegal annexation. It is Putin’s flagship project,” he wrote.

He added: “For years, Russian authorities claimed the bridge was ‘the most protected facility in the world’. Consequently, every successful strike shatters the myth of the invincibility of Russian air defences – as well as the notion that Ukraine is incapable of reaching key targets deep behind enemy lines.”

Ukrainians celebrated on Tuesday with memes. The company Fire Point, which manufactures the Flamingo missile, posted a popcorn emoji. Other social media users shared video of “Kerch Bridge on fire”, a popular song by Saint Javelin which has become an anti-Moscow anthem.

Russian military bloggers were gloomy. One, Russian Engineer, acknowledged the Ukrainian military operation to paralyse the bridge had been “perfect”. Hundreds of unmanned aerial vehicles distracted Russian air defences, he said, before a clinical strike by ballistic missiles.
The attack will further complicate supplies to Crimea, after a summer in which the peninsula struggled with fuel shortages and an intensifying Ukrainian campaign to isolate it from mainland Russia.

Ukraine has for months focused its strikes on the key transport routes supplying Crimea, particularly the so-called Novorossiya highway, a key logistics corridor linking the peninsula to Russia’s Rostov region through the occupied cities of Melitopol and Mariupol.

Russia had already sharply restricted traffic across the Crimean bridge. Moscow has largely stopped using the crossing for rail fuel shipments since the 2022 Ukrainian attack damaged the bridge and set a fuel train ablaze.
Rybar wrote that the latest strike would force Moscow to “completely overhaul” its supply routes to Crimea, shifting more traffic to the Novorossiya highway.
Russia would also have to step up the installation of protective netting along the route, Rybar added, lamenting that the measure had not been introduced in the spring.

Meanwhile in Kyiv, loud explosions could be heard as Russian forces struck two bridges over the Dnipro River. The mayor of the Ukrainian capital, Vitali Klitschko, wrote on Telegram that according to “preliminary information, there have been hits on the north and south bridges in ⁠the capital”. There were water and power cuts in parts of the city, he added later.
Russian forces launched a ​series of attacks on bridges crossing ‌the river earlier this ‌month and in October.
A Russian missile attack injured three people ‌in the region of Cherkasy and also targeted Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second biggest city, local officials said on Telegram.

Russia’s defence ministry claimed ⁠on ⁠Tuesday its ​forces had ⁠carried out a massive ⁠overnight strike ​on ‌Ukrainian ‌military-industrial facilities, ‌transport infrastructure in Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia and the ‌Cherkasy and Dnipropetrovsk regions.
The ministry ​said the strikes also ⁠targeted energy facilities, ​port infrastructure ​and ​vessels ​used ‌by ​Ukraine’s armed ​forces.
The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said earlier on Monday that intelligence showed Russia’s military was planning strikes for Monday evening and throughout Tuesday.
Russian defence ministry data from Monday showed that an overnight Ukrainian drone barrage was the biggest since the start of full-scale war in 2022.

Zelenskyy also said on Monday ⁠that Ukraine had held new online talks with the US presidential envoys ​Steve Witkoff and ​Jared Kushner, as well as European ​representatives, on the prospects of ending the war with Russia.

Kushner ​said progress had been ‌made towards an ​agreement, though important ​challenges remain to end the war, which Russia started by invading Ukraine in February 2022. Moscow annexed the Black Sea Crimea peninsula in 2014.

articles.title: Chaos as crackdown on illegal mining in Guinea causes wave of regional displacement
articles.summary: Ban on illegal artisanal mining triggers mass exodus and diplomatic tensions with neighbouring Sahel states
body: In the border town of Kourémalé, split between Guinea and Mali, thousands of families have been trudging across the frontier over the past week after a sudden ban on illegal artisanal mining triggered a wave of displacement and a regional diplomatic dispute.

Some, like Seydou Traore, a miner in his 30s from Burkina Faso, made the 78-mile trek from Kourémalé to Ouezzindougou, farther inward. Last week, he gathered a small bundle of his belongings and fled Guinea after security forces ordered him and fellow miners to leave.
“We worked hard there, honestly,” he told Agence France-Presse (AFP). “Then one day everything changed. We were told to leave immediately, without even enough time to collect our tools or savings.”

He is among tens of thousands of people displaced across west Africa this month after Guinean authorities enforced the ban, citing the need to curb river pollution and deforestation, caused by large-scale illegal mining across the country, especially in the Siguiri area in the north-east.

In the days that followed, security agents raided mining hotspots, confiscating equipment and arresting 1,263 people. They also expelled thousands more: Mali says up to 160,000 miners fled into the Malian part of Kourémalé and as far as the capital, Bamako. At least six women have given birth in Mali since the displacement began in Guinea.

On 11 November, more than a week later, deadly violence broke out in the Balato community in Siguri, between security agents and miners erecting barricades. At least 10 people were killed and 13 others wounded, and three military vehicles were set alight.

The crackdown has triggered a regional diplomatic dispute: in a statement released on 12 November after a meeting in Ouagadougou, the Alliance of Sahel States said it recognised countries’ authority to enforce their laws, while voicing concern about the decree and expulsions.

Tiffany Wognaih, a senior analyst for the Francophone west and central Africa at geopolitical risk advisory JS Held, said illegal artisanal mining was widespread in the region, “especially in areas that aren’t necessarily continuously monitored by government presence”.
More than 300,000 people in Guinea eke out a living as illegal miners, according to data from the UN Environment Programme.

Many countries in the region lack comprehensive official numbers on gold export and processing. Conakry has remained defiant in the face of its neighbours’ displeasure. Mamady Doumbouya’s administration has grand ambitions to make Guinea a dominant mining force in the region and increase state revenues by tracking most of the value chain for resources such as gold.

The ban on illegal mining was announced a day after Guinea’s first gold refinery, the Nimba Gold Refinery, was officially launched with a declared annual processing capacity of 733 tonnes, far above the country’s annual gold output of 72 tonnes.

“If you’re opening a gold refinery, you need official supplies of gold to flow through the country’s channels,” Wognaih said. “And if a lot of it is being exported out of the country through illegal means and channels, then you don’t have enough processing in the country or showing up on official export figures.”

A year ago, the vast Simandou mine came on stream after nearly three decades of delay, to exploit one of the world’s biggest iron ore deposits. The $20bn project has rapidly ramped up shipments in the run-up to an annual target of 120m tonnes.

Meanwhile, concern is mounting within the Sahel states that the influx will exacerbate a humanitarian crisis that the military juntas are already struggling to contain amid insecurity and soaring living costs.
“These people are vulnerable,” a Malian security ministry official told AFP about the new arrivals. “We are looking at ways to prevent them from being approached by terrorist networks.”

articles.title: Tuesday briefing: Andy Burnham’s government wants to get young people into work. Will cutting their benefits help?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: Guaranteed jobs and expanded employment support sit alongside Alan Milburn’s proposals to cut benefits for some of Britain’s million young people not in education, work or training
body: Good morning. The former health secretary, Alan Milburn, will publish his long-awaited review into the one million young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) later today. The report will propose cutting welfare for some under-25s and spending billions on a new “deal” for young people. The government is at pains to tell you that its approach to welfare is nothing like that of the Tories’: Labour isn’t the party of “crude” benefit cuts, and it sees youth worklessness as a “moral” issue for which young people aren’t to blame.

It’s hard to recall a government report more heavily trailed than this one. It envisages a new relationship between young people and the state, and aims to get more young people into work and education while addressing the cost of young people becoming Neets. But will it work? For today’s First Edition, I spoke to the Guardian’s economics correspondent Richard Partington for a no-nonsense guide to all the things the government will say about this review, and how we should assess their arguments. First, here are the headlines.

UK | The Ministry of Justice has launched an investigation into whether Russell Brand has broken prison rules after the jailed comedian shared a message claiming he was not guilty of sexual offences just days after his conviction.

Israel | The Israeli military uploaded 3.5m photos to Amazon’s cloud platform in order to use the US company’s facial recognition technology to analyse images of Palestinians, the Guardian can reveal.

EU | Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.

UK news | Police chiefs say officers are “retreating from the streets” amid the worst financial crisis in decades, which has left nine forces seeking exceptional financial support (EFS) from the government.
Technology | Microsoft has identified the root causes of the global outage that crippled Outlook, Exchange and a host of other vital office software last week.

Remember when Keir Starmer’s government was forced to back-track last year after backbench Labour MPs voted against its controversial welfare reform bill, which proposed cutting personal independence payments (Pip)? Andy Burnham’s government is keen to avoid a repeat of that scenario, and Milburn has been assiduously trying to win over Labour MPs, as Pippa Crerar wrote yesterday. “The government is taking on an incredibly thorny issue, but they’re presenting this as a way to inject hope for the next generation,” Richard says. “They’re offsetting the negative stuff with a vast increase in employment support.”

Journalists will spend much of this week asking whether Milburn and Burnham have succeeded where Starmer failed. But the real test of their proposals lies far beyond SW1. Neets have been a concern for policymakers since the 1990s, and their number is now higher than ever. Among comparable European nations, only Romania had a higher Neet rate than Britain in 2025. The problem is also unevenly distributed: the likelihood of becoming Neet is (unsurprisingly) far higher in places like Blackpool than in the Cotswolds.

The report tries to address two problems. One is economic: more than a third of Neets do not claim benefits, but the cost of supporting those who do is high. Milburn estimates that £3.2bn of welfare spending on young people who are Neet could be avoided if they were in work. The other is more complex, and reflects a sense of generational despondency among young people, many of whom are “struggling to stay in sync with society at large”, as William Davies wrote in an interesting piece earlier this year (£).
What is Milburn’s review proposing?

• Big changes to welfare for young people: The report proposes the largest overhaul of the benefits system since the creation of universal credit in 2013. It suggests replacing Pip for under-25s and the health element of universal credit with a new “youth allowance”, which would be paid at the standard rate of UC.

• Guaranteed work: In exchange for losing access to their benefits, the government will “guarantee” eligible 18-to-24-year-olds a fully funded, six-month job. This builds on the Starmer government’s jobs guarantee, which was meant to be available to people who had been claiming UC for 18 months. The new proposals would extend eligibility for this to people who have been claiming UC for 12 months.

• More support for young people and employers: Instant (albeit digital) access to mental health support will be provided for young people who are Neet. Employers that hire people who have been Neet for six months will get a payment of £3,000, and the government is also expected to lower national insurance payments by businesses for employees aged between 21 and 24 for a five-year period, starting in retail and hospitality sectors.
What are some of the arguments in favour of these proposals?

Young people don’t want to be out of work. About 84% of young people who are Neet say they want to find a job, education or training. “Being out of work has a huge impact on your sense of wellbeing and mental health, and your finances,” Richard says. A 24-year-old who has never had a job will lose an estimated £300,000 in earnings over their lifetime, even after they enter the labour market. Milburn is proposing an “opportunity” guarantee, giving people support into education, training and work, and a “support” guarantee, allowing them to take this opportunity up. Expect more details on those later today.

Helping young people prepare for work is pointless if nobody wants to hire them. Milburn is expected to make a variation of this argument today. Young people now make up about 40% of the headline unemployment figures, partly because many employers aren’t willing to take a risk on them. But there’s also a risk that paying firms to employ people will benefit companies that would have hired them anyway, effectively handing public money to large corporations that really don’t need it.“Employers have a social responsibility,” Richard says. “But they often make a kneejerk argument for tax cuts and deregulation.”

If you don’t tackle this, your enemies will tackle it for you. The Department for Work and Pensions currently spends 25 times as much on benefits for young people than it does on employment support, something that many MPs believe is unsustainable, even if they find it hard to swallow cuts. “For Labour, there’s a danger that because welfare reform is difficult, it means it should never be touched,” Richard says. “You can imagine a different government taking a very different approach to this.”
What are some of the arguments against them?

Cutting benefits is unnecessary. While the review is being sold as an opportunity for young people, there’s no getting away from the fact that many young people will lose their benefits. About 184,000 young people aged 16 to 24 receive the universal credit health element, some of whom have complex needs that prohibit them from working. Benefits aren’t the cause of people becoming Neet, and if the government was solely interested in creating opportunities for young people, it could do so without cutting welfare. As more people enter the labour market, the number of people on benefits will reduce.

Work doesn’t pay. Governments often treat the labour market as a solution to the rising welfare bill while ignoring the reality of modern work. In-work poverty has been rising over the last decade and many benefit claimants have been forced into low-paid, part-time jobs on zero-hours contracts. As Richard noted earlier this week, countless studies connect badly paid work to poor mental wellbeing. In other words, it’s not enough to funnel young people into jobs. The pay, conditions and quality of those jobs also matter.

Neets are symptomatic of bigger problems. The rate of Neets is higher in disadvantaged and deindustrialised areas where there are fewer jobs. “If there aren’t jobs to go to, what chance of success do you have?” Richard says. In that sense, the proposed changes risk hitting the most disadvantaged the hardest. For the Milburn report’s proposals to work, Richard believes they will need to form part of a wider strategy to create prosperity in places outside the UK’s major cities. Otherwise, the government will simply be managing the consequences of an economic crisis, rather than addressing its cause.

Floods and bombings: Deadly winter approaches in Gaza

Deadly floods in Gaza have created a dire humanitarian crisis, as the governments of Australia, Canada, the UK and Italy call on Israel to allow the safe passage of critical aid to civilians before winter sets in. Tens of thousands of Palestinians in Gaza have been left in waterlogged and damaged tents, with sanitation infrastructure also destroyed by storms. Supplies including food, medicine and water and 150,000 tents are being held by Israel at the border, while the UN warns of the spread of diseases. Lucy Hough speaks to the Guardian’s chief Middle East correspondent, Emma Graham-Harrison.
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

When Georgina Lawton returned to England after a four and a half year stint away in Lisbon, it was depressing at first. She returned in winter, to higher prices and faster pace of life, and a new diagnosis made everything feel that little bit harder. That’s until she picked up a new hobby: ice-skating.

Grabbing some skates and heading to the rink twice a week vastly improved the way she experienced life. Suddenly, life felt full of progress and social connection – and the structure helped with a feeling of aimlessness. She went and bought her first pair of proper skates, and found herself with a new friendship group, aged anywhere from 15-60.
“Friends who had always said I was “all or nothing” joked that I would drop my new hobby when things got tough, but I persisted,” says Lawton.

articles.title: Hundreds arrested in anti-Trump protests in Philippines amid anger over Iran war and AI pact
articles.summary: Organisers say up to 10,000 people could join the next round of demonstrations ahead of the US president’s arrival in Manila for the Asean summit
body: Hundreds of people have been arrested in heated demonstrations against Donald Trump in Manila, as authorities braced for more protests ahead of the US president’s arrival in the city for a leaders’ summit.

Organisers claim as many as 10,000 people will join protests against Trump in the Philippine capital on Tuesday, when he will attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit. The crowds are expected to try to walk to the summit site.
Authorities have arrested nearly 300 people in widespread protests in held in the days leading up to the summit, with large parts of the capital closed off and tight security in place.
Related: Xi, Trump and Putin to discuss ‘world peace’ at trilateral, says China

Some burned effigies of Trump and faced off with police officers armed with batons and shields. Slogans on placards called the American leader the world’s “number one terrorist” in protests held on Monday.

Demonstrators angry at the cost-of-living and energy shock caused by the Iran war, and the new US-led Pax Silica initiative on AI and critical minerals, tried to reach the summit at the Philippine International Convention Center on Monday, but were blocked by police.

Pax Silica has sparked tensions in the Philippines over plans to build a tech hub outside Manila that critics say will affect water and energy supplies, and displace members of the Ayta Indigenous community.
Large sections of central Manila were closed to the public as part of the security cordon, and public holidays instituted for the Asean summit.

Trump will meet with the leaders of Australia, Japan and India on Tuesday night before heading to Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday. There he will attend the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit and hold trilateral talks with China’s president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin of Russia.

The backlash against Trump follows the ouster of Nvidia boss Jensen Huang, and allegations members of the US administration, including the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, knew about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Trump’s delegation was expected to include businessman Elon Musk.

Protest leader Renato Reyes blamed the arrests in Manila on the heavy handed response of the government on the president, Ferdinand Marcos Jr., calling Monday the largest single day of police arrests since Marcos came to office in 2022.
“It is really crazy that the Philippine government is rolling out the red carpet for someone who has been so flatly rejected by the American people,” Reyes said.
“Trump started a war that devastated the global economy and pushed oil prices in the Philippines to historic highs. It has caused untold suffering on the Filipino people.
“So yes, Trump will have to pay for his crimes and he will have to be answerable, not just to the American people, but to the people of the world.”
The Philippine national police said some officers were injured during confrontations with demonstrators opposed to the summit, including when objects were allegedly thrown at officers.
Pax Silica will include a technology hub planned at New Clark City in Tarlac, about 120km from Manila.

Intended to bolster western stocks of AI technology and reduce “excessive dependencies” on single source supply chains, including from China, Pax Silica will provide chips and critical minerals to 25 participating signatory governments.
Amnesty Philippines said demonstrations should not be forcibly or violently dispersed.
“Reports of arrests during the protests demand immediate scrutiny,” director Ritz Lee Santos III said.
“Authorities must explain the specific grounds for each arrest and any continued detention. Anyone detained solely for peacefully exercising their rights must be released immediately.”

articles.title: Serbia’s Student List candidates sworn in as MPs after election triumph
articles.summary: Inaugural parliamentary session comes as ousted populist Aleksandar Vučić threatens mass protests of his own
body: Candidates for Serbia’s Student List, the grassroots movement of political outsiders that pulled off a spectacular victory in last month’s elections over the party of the populist leader Aleksandar Vučić, are to be sworn in as MPs as they begin the process of forming a government.

The 140 candidates – among them academics, lawyers, scientists and the odd actor – will be sworn in on Tuesday during the inaugural session of the new parliament, bringing 14 years of rule by Vučić and his Serbian Progressive party (SNS) to an end.

A caretaker government under the outgoing prime minister, Ðjuro Macut, will remain in office until MPs approve the Student List’s choice of a cabinet. For now, its makeup – including the identity of a future prime minister – remains unclear.
